text: Well, our next guest says investor sentiment is still positive. He also says that there is still lot of cash waiting to re-enter the markets.
Frank La Salla is president of BNY Clearing International and joins us now with more. And Frank, in particular, good morning.

speaker_label: FRANK LA SALLA, PRESIDENT, BNY CLEARING INT'L.
text: Good morning.
I'm wondering how it is that we get solid earnings when we're seeing a lot of warnings about the second half and a lot predictions about slowing economic growth?

Well, you know, I think what's interesting is the way the companies now are really managing expectations. Here's what we have said -- we began this philosophy in the beginning of the year and it seems to be taking shape -- we're going to see slowing growth in the economy, but we're going to see earnings pickup. We had phenomenal first quarter earnings reports. They started to manage our expectations for the second quarter. Second quarter is turning out pretty good, notwithstanding the Amazons and the Nokias of the world, and I think that their setting us up probably for positive surprises on the third. We have to be honest about this, this is what we seem over the past, I would say, eight quarters.
All right, but positive surprises are not necessarily the same as good performance because they do manage expectations.

Yes, the key for the companies is to continued to show quarter over quarter growth. I think the productivity numbers that we were going to see are going to be positive. I think the global story is getting much better. I actually just came back from Europe and I think that, clearly, growth there is picking up, notwithstanding central bank tightenings. I think the economies look very solid in Europe, I think they're going to look much better in Asia. I think that will offset some of the issues we have here in the States with the Fed tightenings. And I think, overall, earnings growth will surprise to the upside. Nothing in the data so far that we've seen suggest that that will change. So again, I think companies are managing expectations. You see what happens when an Amazon and a Nokia, they fall short just on revenues, everybody -- I think it's healthy, and I think that most companies are aware of that, and they want to manage our expectations down. But I still think growth will be positive quarter over quarter.
With global economies behaving so nicely, will it be the large multinational companies that tend to benefit, while the U.S. economy continues to slow?

I think it's going to be two sectors that will probably do better. I think that the multinationals out of the U.S. and even across the world will continue to do well, they will benefit from the global pickup. I also think the small niche-cap, the micro- caps, the small caps, with the Fed now probably on hold, will surprise to the upside as well. A lot of those mid cap, small cap, micro-caps are looking outside of the U.S. for their growth. I think they'll benefit from a global pickup.
With the Fed on hold, how do you feel about financial companies, and particularly investment banks, since we're seeing so much merger and acquisition activity?

Very, very positive. We really like the financial services sector in general. I think that it's a number of issues, a confluence of points. Clearly, with the Fed on hold, as you said, I think that's very, very positive for the financial services. I think the consolidation, or the rationalization, will do well, and I would jump back to Europe on that. Notwithstanding the problems with Dresdner, Commerz, Deutsche that we sell this week in Europe, I think that the merger -- the urge to merge in Europe will continue. I think it's very much on the front plate. And I think it's going to continue to be positive. And I think the spillover will come into the U.S. We'll see more foreign acquisitions of U.S. investment banks and brokers, and I think that's another reason to own this sector.
Yesterday's market activity, the Nasdaq down 3.6 percent, essentially where do you think the money is going, when it is leaving the tech sector?

Well, clearly, the money wants to go back into the stock market. I think that we've learned about the virtue of holding cash, I think that's getting a little old now, and I think we're starting to see it move back. I mean, it's true, we really did. The first half of the year was basically owning cash. I think they better look at the high-quality, profitable companies. I think yesterday's price action was a microcosm of the way we'll see the rally going ahead in the second half; that is to say, a shift to the Dow, S&P; companies, the true profitable companies, companies positioned well with infrastructure to take advantage of this global pickup.
We should note here that that graphic there having the Nasdaq up 19, almost 20 percent since Memorial Day. So we have seen a bit of that summer rally here.

I think the Nasdaq has a lot of work to do. The high -- investors are now really looking under the hood, kicking the tires, before they go in, and the Nasdaq will clearly become much more stock selective then the old S&P;, Dow components.
All right, Frank La Salla, of BNY Clearing International, thank you for being with us this morning.
Good to be here.
The U.S. stocks and bonds rallied Thursday, finishing the month in fine form.
August is typically a sluggish period for the markets, but Thursday's gains makes it the Dow's best month for investors this year.

And joining us now is Frank La Salla, president of BNY Clearing International. A very good performance for the markets in August, even though folks kept saying nothing is going to happen, nothing's going to happen until after Labor Day.

speaker_label: FRANK LA SALLA, PRESIDENT, BNY CLEARING INT'L
text: Actually I was out there hoping we would get this summer rally I was talking about since June.
And we did, so what happens next?

I think we continue. You know, I thought last week, without the Fed having tightened, and we got a good pro-productivity, pro-growth speech out of Greenspan on last Friday, it sort of set the stage for this. So we've had a nice rally going into it. I think it's just -- it's very simply a confluence of the two facts, that the Fed is probably finished, in terms of their tightening cycle, and we're going to probably get better than expected third quarter earnings, numbers from the market. I think the equity market really needs that kind of news to get it going. And I think now, institutional investors particularly, with a lot of cash on their hands, feel much more comfortable about jumping back in. I think we've gotten this rather stealth-like, but clearly nice, move up, bull market again.

Which is interesting too because some of the folks from the trading floor were saying that it felt like the institutional buyer was back in the market the last couple of days. And it's been a retail feel over the past month or so.

It has, and I think one of the reasons why a lot of the guys on the floor probably feel that way is because they see what we see, which is that, you know, this has been broadening out now. This is not just about picking stocks. We're seeing not just the high-techs coming back, the financials coming back, the drugs have had a nice little rally, some of the Internets, the B2B sector and the Internets have come back. That sort of gives us a signal that this is broader-based. There's big money coming back into the market and that's generally institutionally, or institutionally based. So I think that the market's in pretty good shape. And there's no reason to think that, as we get past Labor Day, into September and October, that this rally can't continue.
And will it continue -- so the picture's not really going to change, only the volume numbers are going to come back.

Well, I think that the fundamentals are in place. I think that's right. I think that the earnings picture might actually improve into the fourth quarter. And I think also the important point to remember is that we're seeing this real nice rally in the long end of the treasury curve, that is to say long-term interest rates are coming down. So that'll work its way through the economy and help offset some of the slowdown we're getting now because of the Fed tightenings that we've had over the past 18 months. So, in general, I think that the equity market can do well, but I also think the bond looks very attractive. The 10- and 30-year looks like that will continue to trade low. So dollar-based assets, whether it's dead (ph) or equity, look like they're ready to -- well, will continue to trade better through the end of the year.
Well, let's remember, September and October traditionally are not the warmest and fuzziest months on record for bulls.
Yes, we don't like October at all.
So the question is, where do you want to be positioned, what sort of sectors, heading into the fall, and into the end of the year if we have already seen a nice advance for some groups?

Well, I think that -- I hate to say momentum is back, but it looks like it is coming back. And I don't mean the old momentum, the day trading, buy high, sell higher guys. I mean, really, the growth story. And you know, that is, let's say what we see in the high tech, which I think is, to answer your question, more straight. You know, high tech looks good, financial services still look good, drugs still look good. But in the high-tech era, I think we're looking for companies that have good top-line growth, but also coupled with bottom-line growth. So I think that the old momentum growth plays of buying ideas with no profitability is probably gone. So then you have to look in the high-tech area, where you do see solid profit growth, good top- line growth, and also I think I'd look at some of the -- what were defensive plays, like the drug stocks or the financial services. I think those are real growth stories now. So I'd certainly be looking at those areas.
Russell 2000 also had a great month, up better than, I think, seven percent. Small caps?

That's key, because what -- again, that's the market signaling that the Fed is probably finished. Small caps need liquidity to continue to grow their businesses. And as long as the Fed was in a tightening cycle, there was no way that those stocks were going to do well. Now I think that we've got the all-clear sign from the Fed, I think it's good for small caps. It's actually good for micro caps as well. And I think mid-caps will also benefit from this change in Fed policy, if you will.
OK, the bulls hope you're right, thanks so much.
Thank you.
Frank La Salla, BNY Clearing International.
Well, it was quite an October, and now the major markets began the new month by pausing to catch its breath, retreating slightly following recent strong gains.
That performance did not surprise Wall Street watchers. Here now with more insights is Frank La Salla, president of BNY Clearing International. Good morning. Good to have you with us this morning.

speaker_label: FRANK LA SALLA, PRESIDENT, BNY CLEARING INTL.
text: Good morning.
What is your outlook for the fourth quarter?

Positive. Positive. You know, Deborah, it has been -- since 1995, the last two months of the year have been very, very positive. We've had real sustained rallies. And, you know, when you look at money manager sentiment and the cash on the sidelines, it looks like we are going to get another one of those rallies. I think institutional investors seem very bullish for the right reasons. And I think that a lot of the questions that have kept this market from getting back on its feet are starting to go away, i.e. stable oil, i.e. the election, i.e. whether or not the Fed will ease, which I think they ultimately will. And those things seem to be falling into place. So we might be at a really good point here, in terms of getting this market back on its feet, specifically the Nasdaq, and probably at the end of the day the broader S&P; 500.
And it will set itself up to become attractive enough for people to be pulling money off the sidelines, or are they likely just to be sort of rotating it around the markets?

I think there is enough cash out there where it will probably be broad-based, and the reason I say that is because what we've noticed over the past week is that even the small cap sector has started to base, which tells me that people are really convinced that the Fed is done, and that will be good not just for the big caps, but also for the small caps. So I would expect a broad-based rally here, I wouldn't expected it to be just secular rotation or very narrow leadership taking the market back up.

Let me ask your outlook on two particular sectors, number one, retailing, specifically, apparel retailing; and number two, personal computer sales, both of those things find the fourth quarter as the most important profits period.

It is. And, you know, we got some numbers yesterday. I guess the retail industry came out, they are suggesting that we will get good Christmas sales. I'll tell you, I have been very, very sanguine on the retail sector, and it is not so much because of consumer demand, but more because of pricing power. Retailers simply have no pricing power. And, you know, we got consumer sentiment this week, it really wasn't that great either. So it's hard to make a case that the retailers are going to have an exceptionally good fourth quarter. It will probably be OK, but at the end of the day, I think retailers really have a tough way to go here and I would really be avoiding this sector as an investment.
What about the PC makers?

I think, you know, the semiconductor, you know, as you reported before, I think the semiconductor industry seems a little bit more upbeat. I thought the news out of Intel last night was positive. I do think that story is better because of the global pickup. Europe probably has already made its investments for the next six to eight months, but Asia really has been lagging. My guess will be, if we see a pickup in growth in Asia, which still has to materialize, I think PC sales will pick up and I think profitability will be OK. Companies like Dell look like they are probably in good shape to get a rally if that happens, but I would not put my bet down today, I would sort of spread it out.
The stock market has long been a leading indicator, has it factored in a Bush victory?

I'll tell you, as the week progresses, it seems to me that the Street is bracing not just for a Bush victory, but for a clean sweep for the Republicans. It looks like the Street is getting more confident that we will see Congress, obviously, the Senate seems to be a lock anyway, but Congress and the White House will go to the Republicans. And surprisingly enough, the markets held in pretty well. We would have thought that they may have gotten a little bit nervous. You know, we like gridlock, we like do no harm. We like things to be muddled in Washington. It works well, it worked well from -- if you look at from '94, you know, when the Democrats lost the House and, you know, they had the Senate, we had a nice rally. I think, though, this time the Street feels that the victory will be so marginal that if the Republicans take a sweep, they won't be able to do too much too fast, and I think that is why the market has been pretty OK with the way it looks like it is going to turn out.
Frank La Salla, BNY Clearing International, great to have you with us this morning.
Good to be here.
How tough can it be for the markets in 2001 to surpass their performance in 2000? After all, the Nasdaq knocked about 40 percent off its value last year. The Dow was down about 6 percent.
Get a reading on that front from Frank La Salla, president of BNY Clearance International. Welcome, Happy new year to you.

speaker_label: FRANK LA SALLA, BNY CLEARANCE INTERNATIONAL
text: Happy new year.
Looking forward to a better year this year than last?
Yes, always looking forward.
What will be different about it?

You know, it's funny. Forecasting is a -- it's got a spiritual component to it. It's exercising humility. And I think a lot of us went through that last year. And, you know, I was thinking about it on the way over here. Last year I was saying -- a year ago today -- we would see a declining economy, you know, GDP growth would slow, but earnings would expand. So I got it half right. I think this year, though, might be a little different. I think that even though we're talking about recession, you know, Deborah, you said the "all" word, everybody's a little concerned, I think we're going to see the economy expand through the rest of 2001. But I also think, simultaneously, we'll see earnings growth also expand. I think that we have two really good levers right now. We certainly have to talk of tax cuts coming out of the new administration. And probably more importantly, the Fed has put itself in a position where we can really get a nice amount of liquidity coming into the economy. And we get a resumption in capital expenditures. Now that we've sort of worked through Y2K, we've gotten through the year 2000, I think we're going to see high-tech expenditures increase. So we're going to get renewed leadership in the Nasdaq companies, and I think that'll be positive. So, overall, the set up for the stock market, I think, is very, very positive right now.
All right, there are some negatives, though, notably investor nervousness after a shellacking a lot of people took last year.
Yes.
What would it take to change investor psychology? And where does a Fed rate cut figure into that?

Well, I think that we've all talked about the Fed rate cut. I think it's just -- it's certainly not a matter of whether or not they're going to do, it's clearly a matter of when and the effectiveness of the rate cut. So my sense is, from an investor psychology standpoint, that the cuts were already in the market. If you look at the April Fed, futures Fed funds rate, it's actually suggesting 75 basis points. I think that's very reasonable. I think institutional investors are going to lead the way back into this. In other words, I think retail clients have gotten hurt. It was always by the dips. Well, we had four dips last year and, you know, they're still waiting for the rally. So I think institutional investors who are very, very bullish here, who have a lot of cash, will bring us back into the market, and probably do it going into the end of January meeting. I think that'll be positive. And then the retail investor will probably feel more comfortable about coming into the market, and then I think we'll see a real long-term rally with both retail and institutional money coming back into the equity market.
To make money in the market this year, will it be as easy as just buying the really battered up text stocks that were down so bad last year?

No, I really don't. I think that the -- I think, first of all, I think the era of over-investing is finished. I think that the frenzy that we saw in '98 and '99 are over. Now, that doesn't mean we won't have a nice full market. That doesn't mean the Nasdaq can't have another 80 percent rally, but what it does mean is that I think investors are going to go into this more soberly. I think you're going to see the broader market indices do well. But on a company-by-company basis, I think stock picking gets very, very difficult and needs to be done very carefully. Because of the changes in the economy, because what we're seeing in global pickup, because of the specialties in high tech which have led this, it becomes a different way of investing going forward.
OK, you can't just throw money at the market or at the indices. What sectors would you concentrate on?

Well, we've been very bullish on drugs and financials for a long time, and a lot of people on the Street have and I think that's worked out very well. We're starting to look at the high techs again, specifically the Nasdaq 100s. But for right now, until we get rate cuts from the Fed and we see what the tax plan looks like, we're going to recommend a defensive posture, which is still drugs, financial services. Within financial services, insurance companies look good on a fundamental basis. Certainly broker dealers have gotten beat up in the past couple of quarters. We think that's certainly a place to look as well.

We've seen within the telecoms names like AT&T; just get hammered away. Its cousin there, Lucent Technologies, also just had a just a bad year last year as well. Are we going to be sitting here a year from now wishing that we'd bought those stocks?

Well, I think some of them. Lucent is certainly, in my mind, a different company than AT&T.; The luster came off of Lucent this year. The luster has been off of AT&T; for a number of years. AT&T; reminds me a lot of IBM in the late '80s -- actually maybe even the mid '80s. You know, it was sort of a company that was floundering, it was a value stock, then it became a growth stock, then it became a value stock, then it went back to a growth stock again. I think AT&T; can do that. I like Michael Armstrong. I think he's done a lot on cutting expenses. What he has not been able to do is convince the Street that he can raise revenues. If he can do that -- and I think he can -- we will be here 12 months from now saying, I should have bought AT&T; on Jan. 2.
We'll see. We'll have you back before then. We'll hold you to it.
Thank you.
Frank La Salla, BNY Clearing International, thanks.
Happy new year.
As you know, the Fed cut interest rates, as expected, by 50 basis points yesterday.
And Frank La Salla is president of BNY Clearing International, here to give his thoughts on the Fed actions and what they might mean for the stock market. Good morning, Frank.

speaker_label: FRANK LA SALLA, PRESIDENT, BNY CLEARING INTERNATIONAL
text: Good morning, David.
Good time at this point to be committing fresh money to the stock market, or do you sort of hang back and wait for further clarification of the weakness that we're seeing in the economy?

Yes, I mean, you know, that's a good point. The short answer to your question is is yes, I think now is the time to really look back into the equity market. Obviously, the right time was back in December, when it was really bad. You know, the stock -- especially Nasdaq -- had given a nice thank you with, I guess, about 15 percent up for the month since we had the first rate cut, in early January. So, you know, we're going to go through a tough period now. Not a horrendous period -- but the fact is is the Fed has given us basically about as much as it can in terms of liquidity. I don't think Greenspan could have done much more than the 50 basis points he did. If it had been 75, I don't think the market would have rallied that much more for you -- then 25, we certainly would have sank. I think my sense now is we've got to see the economic data begin to convince us that the recovery has begun, and until that happens it's very hard to make a case for another big move up in equity prices.

We're going to get an APM. We're going to also get a jobs report this week. These are important numbers -- in fact, it was the NAPM report that many think is what prompted the Fed to cut between meetings last time around. If we still get a lot of weakness, could we see an inter-meeting move? The Fed doesn't have a meeting until late March.

You know, it's funny -- I -- well, you're right about a couple of things. One is the NAPM is key, because Greenspan always looks at NAPM, and more importantly now, it's the first piece of reliable data we will get for the month of January. See, the third quarter -- well, actually, the most important numbers were the December numbers, and a lot of them are estimated, simply because of the way, the mechanics, of how they calculate it work -- so the NAPM report becomes that much more important. I don't think, however, that Greenspan will do an inter-meeting cut, because if he does that, politically, I think it will be viewed as he looking at stock prices, which is what he's been accused and said he's not doing. So my feeling would be is we've got 100-basis point cuts now. He's going to give it a chance to work through the economy, and he'll continue to monitor the data. But the interesting thing about the NAPM report will be how was January, how bad was January. And on the heels of the consumer confidence and business confidence numbers that we got earlier, you know, a couple of days ago, it'll be very important to give us a gauge as to how December and January are shaping up in terms of growth.
It's expected to be weak.

It is. And, honestly, the data is still bad. In other words, business -- consumer confidence was really bad -- and business confidence was bad, and business confidence generally leads consumer confidence.
Right.

It's a long way of saying I think consumer confidence is going to go down a little bit more before it goes up. So the data is going to be bad, but I think Greenspan knows a lot of this has to work itself through the economy. So like I said, he may come in with some system repose, pump some high-powered liquidity into the system. A retroactive tax cut will certainly help as well. But I wouldn't be looking for anymore rate cuts right now. And I think the market will probably trade better, but again, as I said before, I don't think we're going to have these dramatic moves up that we may have seen, even in the month of January.
Trading better because it's a forward-looking indicator?

Yes, I mean, you know, equity prices are leading. I mean, you know, they -- if they do their job, projecting the economy six months from now -- look, the first half of the year is bad. That's baked in the cake. The question becomes how good can the third and fourth quarter of this year be? My hunch is as nonlinear as the slowdown was in 2000 for the economy, it could as nonlinear on the upside. It's very possible, if we get enough liquidity, capital expenditures may increase more than we think they are now. That will be very, positive, and then equity prices will, obviously, resume on the upside.
There still are worries about a recession. You don't think we're headed right down into one? You think it's going to come back?

Yes, I mean, the numbers that we run suggests that we might get as low as zero, probably half a percent at the worse case, in the real trough, and that can happen in the first quarter or maybe the second quarter. But we don't see negative growth. We certainly don't see back-to-back negative growth. We think the economy's resilient enough and capital flows are strong where we might be able to avert any negative growth. It'll be slow, but then we might get a nice rally in the second half of the year.
All right, Frank, good to see you.
Thank you.
Frank La Salla, BNY Clearing International.
Well, futures markets are indicating we may see a bit of a bounce up in stock prices today, which has to be a relief, after the sinking we saw last week.
Yes, it wasn't very pretty. Frank La Salla, president of BNY Clearing International, is here with us this morning -- welcome, good morning to you.
Good morning.

speaker_label: FRANK LA SALLA, PRESIDENT, BNY CLEARING INTERNATIONAL
text: Good morning.
It was all -- it was awhile ago, Friday, of course, but we did have a five-percent drop in the Nasdaq. What was the message sent out by that decline, and do you think we can rebound from here?

Well, I think we can, but certainly, you know, the earnings numbers we got in the telecommunications sector really confirm the greatest fear we all have, and that is we're in a profit recession, and that's basically what we're going through now. So we have this confluence of bad earnings in some of the best industries that we can think, like wireless, for example, coupled with this real slowdown in the economy. The data just gets worse and worse. I don't want to paint a terrible picture, because I think it's going to get better. But the fact is is that those are the things that really concern the market, especially the Nasdaq. So, when you get that kind of information, you get that kind of data -- it's what we talked about a few weeks ago: We're going to get bad news, we're probably going to get bad news for another four or five weeks -- presents a buying opportunity, because I think the good news is that we are getting liquidity. It seems to me, given the pick up in monetary aggregates, that we might be in the trough right now, and that is the time you really want to buy equities, right before the economy starts to pick up.
All right, what would you look at it?

Well, I certainly think wireless, for example, certainly presents a good opportunity for a lot of people. I don't think that it's the end of the world for wireless. There are certain concerns about earning, but companies like WorldCom, companies like Nortel, even Corning, for example, which was down, I guess, nine points on Friday, certainly present opportunities for people who are going to be in that sector for the long run. I don't think it's gone. And if you believe the economy is going to pick up, you have to believe that subscribers will -- subscribership will continue to grow in the United States. It will certainly continue to grow in Europe. And so it presents a really good opportunity for long-term investors.
How do you feel about the retailers, as we swing out of this trough?

You know, I can't win on the retailers. Every time I think I've got the retailers figured out -- retailers have it tough: Whether it's the Internet or whether it's traditional retailers, the fact is is that I see no signs of their ability to get any pricing power back. And so because of that, whether or not the economy is good or not really doesn't matter, because retailers have a tough go even when the economy was roaring. So my sense is retailers are going to have to retool. There will probably be more consolidation, and the old clicks and bricks will probably continue to come together. But overall, it's very hard to make a case for retailing, only because of the changing dynamics of the economy and the influence of the Internet. So I would -- I would stand clear of retailers, only because I certainly haven't had a good call on them -- and I really don't see too much upside growth, you know.
Even with presumably a tax cut coming and the Fed cutting interest rates -- looks good for consumer spending.

Oh, it's going to be great for consumer spending, and I think consumer sentiment might be hitting bottom now: You might get one more bad number. So I think psychologically it's good. But again, when consumer spending was up and the economy was roaring, retailers were still having a tough go of it. You get some specialty places, like, I guess, like the Targets of the world: They seem to be able to do well. But you've really got to be able to pick those companies really, really good. And I certainly can't say I know which are going to come out ahead and which aren't.
When you look at technology -- we were flipping through the paper earlier: There's a full-page ad by one of the box makers, you know, essentially selling you a computer and a free printer for $699...
Right.

... as you look at the box makers and the tech group as a whole, are you attracted to them? Are you going to wait for them? Are they going to be the ones that lead us out of this time right now, or do you wait and sort of let them pick up a little bit?

I would certainly be buying. I'm a believer that until technology moves up and starts to really take the lead, the whole broader market can't move. So I do believe in technology. What is a bit of a concern is that every day we get news that another 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 layoffs are coming, and so what I get a sense of is Alan Greenspan's actually been very bullish, while the market's falling apart, which is sort of ironic. But the fact is is this great productivity machine that we've built seems to be having some problems right now. So between the layoffs and between the flat-line capital expenditures that we see -- you know, no one's really spending in technology -- I think it's going to be a rough go for the technology sector, but you have to believe in the long run it will be OK, there will be more capital expenditures, people will go back to work, the productivity machine will come back -- and I think the technology sector will lead again: It's just going to take a little time.
Thank you, Frank La Salla, BNY Clearing.
Thank you.
